name: Migraine

matching.reasoningTemplate: Recurrent headache with photophobia and nausea, no fever or meningism, favours primary migraine.

redFlags: New focal deficit, thunderclap onset, or fever → exclude secondary cause

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e Ch.441 p.3462-3471 (Migraine and Other Primary Headache Disorders); Ch.17 p.113-116 (Headache); Ch.34 p.230 (Disorders of the Eye); Ch.433 p.3379; Ch.437 p.3429
clinicalPearls: Migraine is the second most common cause of headache and the leading neurologic cause of disability worldwide; over a 1-year period it affects roughly 15% of women and 6% of men (p.3462).
An attack classically evolves through three phases - premonitory (prodrome), headache, and postdrome - and only about 20-25% of patients also experience an aura phase (p.3462).

Premonitory symptoms (yawning, sleepiness, fatigue, cognitive 'fog', mood change, neck discomfort, polyuria/polydipsia, food cravings) can begin hours to days before the pain; some apparent 'triggers' such as light sensitivity may actually be part of this early phase rather than true precipitants (p.3462).
Postdromal tiredness, poor concentration and mild neck discomfort can persist for hours and occasionally up to a day after the pain settles (p.3462).

Simplified diagnostic criteria require repeated attacks of headache lasting 4-72 h with a normal examination and no other reasonable cause, plus at least 2 of (unilateral, throbbing, aggravated by movement, moderate/severe) and at least 1 of (nausea/vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia) (Table 441-3, p.3466).

Cranial autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, periorbital swelling, ptosis) can occur in migraine - even in children - and may be mistaken for sinus disease, leading to overdiagnosis of sinusitis and inappropriate treatment (p.114).

Migraine is a brain disorder, not a 'vascular headache'; vascular changes when present are secondary, driven by cranial parasympathetic activation, and treatment response cannot be predicted by vascular effects (p.114).

The vast majority of patients presenting with severe headache have a benign cause, most often migraine; brain tumor is a rare cause of isolated headache and an even rarer cause of severe pain (p.114).

Migraineurs do not encounter more stress than headache-free people; the problem is overresponsiveness to changes in stress, and they are characteristically sensitive to environmental/sensory stimuli, failing to habituate easily (p.3462, p.3508).
Vertigo can be a prominent migraine feature - about one-third of patients referred for vertigo/dizziness have a primary diagnosis of migraine (vestibular migraine) (p.3464).
harrison.pathophysiology: Migraine is understood as a brain disorder of sensory processing rather than a primary vascular disease. The characteristic sensory sensitivity is attributed to dysfunction of monoaminergic and other sensory-control systems in the brainstem and hypothalamus. The key nociceptive pathway is the trigeminovascular system: trigeminal innervation of large intracranial vessels and dura, with terminals that, when activated, release vasoactive neuropeptides - notably calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) - at vascular terminals and within the trigeminal nucleus. Second-order neurons of the trigeminocervical complex (caudal trigeminal nucleus extending into the upper cervical dorsal horns, receiving C1-C2 input) decussate and project via the quintothalamic tract to ventrobasal and posterior thalamic nuclei, with additional projections to periaqueductal gray and hypothalamus that exert descending antinociceptive modulation; the dorsal raphe nucleus, locus coeruleus, parabrachial nucleus and rostroventromedial medulla are implicated in this modulation. Serotonin (5-HT) is involved - triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists (some also 5-HT1F) and ditans are selective 5-HT1F agonists - and dopamine contributes, with dopamine-receptor hypersensitivity in migraineurs. Functional imaging shows hypothalamic activation in the premonitory phase and persistent dorsolateral pontine (including locus coeruleus) activation during attacks and in chronic migraine, with lateralization correlating with the side of head pain. Genetic study of familial hemiplegic migraine implicates ion channels (CACNA1A/Cav2.1 P/Q calcium channel in FHM1 ~50%; ATP1A2 Na-K ATPase in FHM2 ~20%; SCN1A sodium channel in FHM3), suggesting altered membrane excitability predisposes to aura. The slowly advancing visual scotoma with luminous (fortification) edges is recognized as a marker of spreading cortical depression associated with migraine (p.3462-3464, p.3379).
additionalDifferentials: Tension-type headache - the main differential; distinguished by being completely featureless (no nausea/vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia, throbbing or aggravation with movement), whereas migraine has one or more of these (p.3471).
Cluster headache and other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (p.3462).
Acephalgic migraine / typical aura without headache - recurrent neurologic symptoms with little or no headache (p.3464).
Vestibular migraine - common, underdiagnosed cause of episodic vertigo lasting minutes to hours, sometimes without headache (p.3464).
Migraine with brainstem aura (formerly basilar/basilar-type migraine) (p.3464).
Medication-overuse headache complicating an underlying migraine tendency (p.115-116).
infectionMimics: Bacterial/viral meningitis - acute severe headache with stiff neck and fever; can be mistaken for migraine because pounding headache, photophobia, nausea and vomiting are shared cardinal features, and there is often striking accentuation of pain on eye movement; lumbar puncture is mandatory (p.113-114).
nonInfectiousMimics: Subarachnoid hemorrhage / ruptured aneurysm, AVM or intraparenchymal hemorrhage - thunderclap headache maximal in under 5 min lasting over 5 min, stiff neck without fever; CT may rarely be normal so LP may be needed (p.114).

Brain tumor - intermittent deep dull aching, may worsen with exertion or position change and cause nausea/vomiting; vomiting preceding headache by weeks is highly characteristic of posterior fossa tumors (p.114).

Temporal (giant cell) arteritis - dull/boring headache with superimposed stabbing pains, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, polymyalgia, fever, weight loss in patients over ~50; migraineurs may report relief with prednisone, confounding interpretation of treatment response (p.114-115).
Acute angle-closure glaucoma - prostrating headache with nausea/vomiting beginning with severe eye pain; red eye with a fixed, mid-dilated pupil (p.115).
Transient ischemic attack / vertebrobasilar insufficiency - acute homonymous visual symptoms with fogging/graying and positive phenomena that can mimic migraine aura (p.230).
Ischemic stroke - migraine can mimic stroke even without prior migraine history, especially acephalgic migraine (p.3429).
additionalInvestigations: Migraine is a clinical diagnosis in patients with a normal examination and no other reasonable cause for headache (Table 441-3, p.3466).
A headache diary aids diagnosis and quantifies disability and attack frequency (p.3462).
The Migraine Disability Assessment Score (MIDAS) is a validated tool to grade disability (p.3465).

CT or MRI of the brain (equally sensitive as initial screen for intracranial pathology) is indicated for an abnormal neurologic examination or recent-onset headache; lumbar puncture may additionally be required when a benign cause cannot otherwise be established (p.113).

General acute-headache workup may include palpation of cranial arteries, assessment of the cervical spine, blood pressure and urine examination, and funduscopy with intraocular pressure measurement (p.113).
redFlags: Sudden-onset (thunderclap) headache or first/worst-ever severe headache (p.114).
Subacute worsening over days or weeks (p.114).
Pain induced by bending, lifting or cough (p.114).
Pain that disturbs sleep or is present immediately on awakening (p.114).
New headache in a patient with a known systemic illness (e.g., malignancy) (p.114).
Pain with local tenderness, e.g., over the temporal artery (p.114).
harrison.prognosis: Patients should understand that migraine is an inherited tendency to headache that can be modified and controlled by lifestyle measures and medication but not eradicated. Except on some occasions in women taking oral estrogens or contraceptives, migraine is not associated with serious or life-threatening illness (p.3464). Migraine is nonetheless the most common neurologic cause of disability worldwide (p.3462). Recognized complications (ICHD-3) include status migrainosus, persistent aura without infarction, migrainous infarction, and migraine aura-triggered seizure; migraine may also progress to chronic migraine (Table 441-1, p.3463). Overuse of acute analgesics can transform episodic migraine into refractory medication-overuse headache; many patients improve after withdrawal, though residual headache often persists reflecting the underlying primary disorder (p.115-116).
pitfalls: Mistaking migraine-related cranial autonomic symptoms for sinusitis, leading to overdiagnosis and inappropriate sinus treatment (p.114).
Misdiagnosing meningitis as migraine (or vice versa) because pounding headache, photophobia, nausea and vomiting overlap - hence LP is mandatory when fever and stiff neck are present (p.113-114).
Attributing a steroid-responsive headache in an elderly patient to giant cell arteritis when migraine (far more prevalent in the elderly) also improves with prednisone (p.115).

Treating headache from a reawakened migraine syndrome (e.g., after otologic or endodontic procedures) without first addressing the primary problem - the headache stays refractory until the cause is treated (p.113).

Failing to recognize acephalgic migraine, which can present de novo even after age 65 and is easily confused with stroke; the sensory/motor deficit migrates slowly across a limb over minutes (versus seconds in stroke) (p.3429).
Continuing acute analgesics while starting a preventive - a common cause of treatment failure and of medication-overuse headache (p.115-116).
harrison.severityClassification: ICHD-3 (IHS 2018) classifies migraine into migraine without aura, migraine with aura (typical aura with/without headache, migraine with brainstem aura, hemiplegic migraine including FHM1-3 and sporadic, retinal migraine), chronic migraine, complications of migraine (status migrainosus, persistent aura without infarction, migrainous infarction, migraine aura-triggered seizure), probable migraine, and episodic syndromes that may be associated with migraine (cyclical vomiting, abdominal migraine, benign paroxysmal vertigo/torticollis, infantile colic, vestibular migraine). Chronic migraine is defined as migraine on 8 or more days per month with at least 15 total headache days per month (Table 441-1, p.3463; p.3462). Disability is graded by MIDAS: Grade I 0-5, Grade II 6-10, Grade III 11-20, Grade IV over 20 (Fig. 441-4, p.3466).
